utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we resume the examination of the current witness, the Chamber informs the parties that Judge Nieto-Navia is ill, and the illness is likely to be of a short duration. And therefore, the remaining Judges, Judge El Mahdi and myself after having consulted Judge Nieto-Navia have decided that it is in the interests of justice to proceed, and as the parties know, Judge Nieto-Navia will have an opportunity to read the literal transcript of these hearings and will be able, if needed, to look at the videorecording and the audiorecording of these hearings. So we will proceed this afternoon with just two Judges. There are a few issues I'd like to discuss with the parties, but not until the moment where we have finished the examination of the first witness. So may I ask you, Madam usher, to escort Mr. DP1 into the courtroom. And I'd like to get the confirmation that the facial distortion is still effective, even when the witness enters the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. DP1. May I remind you you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave the day before yesterday, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Ierace, please proceed and cross-examine the witness. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like -- could -- the technicians seem to have problems. Thank you very much. I didn't want to interrupt Mr. Ierace once he has done the interrogation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The technicians have problems, or?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that I do not know, Mr. President. But I have a technical problem with my monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I could be the second in the queue for my laptop. Let's proceed. You have the transcript on your screen, so we will ask the technicians to help us with the laptop computers. Mr. Ierace. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You told us that you lived in Sarajevo and were there until July of 1994. As you walked around Sarajevo in those war years before July 1994, is it the case that everywhere on the roads, on the foot paths, there were the impact marks of mortars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In quite a number of places.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: They were throughout the city, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those areas where I moved around, yes, to a considerable degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1992 and thereafter, barricades were erected on intersections to protect civilians as they crossed the roads from snipers, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, in my part of the city, there were only some paths which took you between the buildings, and in that part of the city, I did not see any barricades. The first time I saw them, and they were huge, was when I left Sarajevo to Padine [phoen], Trebevic, to Lukavica. There was a huge sheet of cloth which had been put up there, and I was told that it was to screen us from snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Whereabouts was that barricade, that sheet of cloth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you get down -- go down the road from Vrace towards the former barracks, to the right, were posts and this sheet of cloth was hung between those posts. And I saw them the first time when I went out. But they were so-called anti-sniper paths. That is what people called them, including the part of the city where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And those anti-sniping paths were routes for civilians to cross the city safely so they were not exposed to sniper fire from positions held by the Bosnian Serb army, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: People believed that this would provide protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to this question, Your Honours, because it is incredibly leading. It is based on the principle that it is a Serb army which fired and that one had to be protected against Serb shots. My objection is based on the fact that we believe that they were simply shots, also within the city. So a question phrased in this manner is not acceptable. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, would you like to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The objection misunderstands the nature of cross-examination. The fact that it is leading is not a proper basis for objecting when the question is put in cross-examination. In any event, the witness's answer accommodates the part of the concern expressed by my learned colleague. But fundamentally, there is nothing wrong with that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I think it's already a couple of months ago that we had a very short discussion on leading questions and whether they were allowed or not. And it's my recollection that I then explained to you that that was exactly the difference between examination-in-chief and cross-examination, that in examination-in-chief, questions should not be leading; and at least that the other party could object against leading questions although very often they slip through because they are not on the contested issues. Cross-examination, leading questions, in general, are permitted. So the objection is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, the city, prior to July 1994, and since the beginning of the armed conflict, was in a large part surrounded by forces of the Bosnian Serb Army, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And I suggest to you there can be no doubt that from their positions, the Bosnian Serb army launched shells and fired into the city?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I could gather, and that is also part of my previous answer, the city was divided. There were parts controlled by Serbs and parts controlled by Muslim forces. And it is not in dispute that there was fierce fighting between them, and that included also the shelling of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, you have no doubt in your mind do you that the Bosnian Serb Army forces fired into the city, that is the part of the city that was on the side of the confrontation lines controlled by the presidency. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And that gunfire was often targeted against civilians, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to make such a claim. I have neither information nor knowledge of that. But I'm quite sure that there was fighting between them and very fierce at that. And that weapons were involved. But whether they were targeting military objectives or civilians, that is something I cannot say because you insisted that I tell you only about what I saw with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm insisting about what I saw with your own eyes, and what you as a reasonable person concluded as someone who lived in the city in those years. I suggest to you it was obvious that there were places you could not go without placing yourself in danger of being shot, and that those places were areas which were open to the view of the areas controlled by the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no doubt that in these clashes and during the shelling, there had to be civilian casualties. In modern parlance, it is called collateral damage. Yes, there were civilian casualties, and I said Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. already yesterday that I had seen such victims personally on Miskin Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And they were civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were they men and women?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, both. According to the list that was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier the routes that developed for civilians to pass through the city. Those routes were heavily used by pedestrians, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you use those routes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now and then, yes. Among other things, because they were also shortcuts. They went through some passages going around certain streets. And I frequently used a particular path when I went to visit my sister because that was indeed a shortcut.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, do you seriously tell us that the only reason you used those routes was because they were a convenient shortcut and not for your own protection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, during those 800 days in Sarajevo, there were really very many days when one could walk freely around the streets. And I told you only what I used going to one particular destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, I suggest you have not answered my question. I will repeat it. Do you seriously tell us that the only reason you used those routes was because they were a convenient shortcut and not for your own protection?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to the use of the word "seriously." I believe that -- what shall I call it? It is an attitude which is not acceptable because it has negative implications. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. Nevertheless, some guidance, Mr. Ierace. Whenever we could avoid words that might -- whenever we could avoid, since it's not necessary, to use words that might have a certain impact on a witness, the Chamber very much would appreciate if you would do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There was a route, a safety route, that was particularly used by pedestrians to move through the city in a east/west direction. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there were places where nothing was protected, and one knew that one could expect shots there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The obvious reason I suggest to you for taking that particular route was that if pedestrians did not take the protection of the buildings which it offered, they were then exposed to Bosnian Serb army positions to the south of the city. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you say "that was the opinion" do you mean that that was the obvious reason that many people used that route?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, everybody has an instinctive fear and collective consciousness, and that is how they behave. There was a general belief that there was a threat of shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It was a common sight, I suggest to you, to see civilians running across exposed intersections where there were not protective barriers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the early months, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You talked about periods of time when people could move freely. Were they the cease-fires?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I take it that you moved freely during the cease-fires. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, depends on who did what and where everybody was. But people moved quite a lot around the city, and as far as I know, if my memory serves me well, there were about -- there were some 19 cease-fire agreements. And one can't say that they were really respected all the way at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: My question is quite simple: Did you personally move freely during the cease-fires?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you take advantage of the cease-fires to get out more from the protection of where you lived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except those occasions when, because of the illness, I had to be at home, I had to go out every day during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Are you saying that up until July 1994, you had to leave your home every day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I had things to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. I see. Now, you, I take it, had a large number of friends and acquaintances in Sarajevo during that period of time who regarded themselves Bosnian Serbian. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were those and the others and others again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps you, sir, more than many others had a wide circle acquaintances of Bosnian Serbs living in Sarajevo. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have to turn to closed session. Private session. Yes, private session will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, you've told us that you attended two funerals during the armed conflict where the deceased was from the Bosnian Serb community, that is, two funerals you attended in Sarajevo. Where were each of the deceased buried?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both buried in the old Orthodox cemetery. The name escapes me. It goes along the road from which goes from Sarajevo to Vogosca behind the Kosevo park.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Which funeral parlour was involved with those two funerals?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, bearing in mind the protective measures, I wouldn't want us to go from parlour and cemetery. We will then be more accurate about the places. I don't know whether we should go into closed session or not. But I thought I would just mention this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There's no need for that, Mr. President. There's nothing in that question that could remotely raise a closed session issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber does not discern at this very moment any reason to go into closed session. Please proceed, and I take it Mr. Ierace you will be as careful as I expect from the parties to keep in mind that when necessary to go into private or closed session. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President. Excuse me, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. What was the funeral parlour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately at the time, Orthodox funeral associations were not operating. There was one in the old town, but it wasn't operating as such. So these were privately organised funerals.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What time of day or night did the funerals take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were both during the daytime, usual time in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And these were Orthodox funerals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of Orthodox funerals being conducted in the nighttime during the armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think the answer was no.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the answer was no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: With all your contacts during the armed conflict, as far as you're aware, an Orthodox funeral was never targeted. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In both cases, when I went to the funeral, there was no shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That's not the question, sir. With all of your contacts during the armed conflict, as far as you're aware, an Orthodox funeral was never targeted. Is that your position? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear about that. I said I would be speaking about what I saw, and I went to two funerals and there was no shooting and I never heard about anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: DP1, the question now is whether you ever heard from another person of an Orthodox funeral being attacked. So the question is now not about what you -- whether you experienced yourself an attack on a funeral you attended, but whether you heard of an attack on Orthodox funerals. Would you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard about any.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of an Orthodox funeral taking place at night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. As far as you're aware, there was no reason for an Orthodox funeral procession to take place at night. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear that any funerals took place at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I take it the answer is that you never heard of an Orthodox funeral procession --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I must interrupt. I believe that I heard the witness say in his own language that other funerals, which doesn't come out from the English transcript, because the way that I understand was that any funerals is what it says in the transcript. What the witness is saying is that he means that other funerals didn't take place at night. Perhaps the question could be asked again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The suggestion was that the question would be asked again. May I invite you to answer the questions as they are put to you. So if the question is whether you ever heard about an Orthodox funeral taking place at night you answer if you ever heard about that or not. If the Prosecution is interested to know whether a similar thing would have happened with other funerals, they will certainly ask you for any additional information. But it was your answer that, at least to this question about Orthodox funeral processions, was your answer that you never heard of any funeral, whether Orthodox or not, took place during the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. night? Is that the answer you -- because the translation might not be perfect. That was your answer? Yes. May I also invite you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- To say yes. That can be translated. Nodding is very difficult to translate as you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yesterday you were asked some questions by the Defence counsel about the condition of two mosques in the area where you lived. And you told us that they were not shelled prior to July 1994. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I understood the question that the attorney asked me, whether they were damaged, and I know for sure they were not damaged because I went past them almost every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I suggest to you that there were mosques in Sarajevo which prior to July 1994 were damaged and in some cases destroyed by shelling. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. I didn't see it. I saw these two mosques. And I also some others in the city which were also not damaged. But it is possible that there were some that were damaged. Because I didn't go to all the areas in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In the first phase of the war, a number of public buildings, in particular, important buildings, were shelled and destroyed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I even observed the shelling of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What about the library? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to object here. I remember in the past that the questions in relation to the library that Mr. Ierace wanted to ask were not accepted by the Chamber, I believe, because this happened much before than the period in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace, before answering, first of all your question was about the first phase. It was to the Chamber not entirely clear what the first phase would precisely comprise. And would you then also please respond to the objection of Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The Prosecution has not previously sought to elicit any evidence in relation to the destruction of public buildings including places of worship for reasons that I explained to the Trial Chamber yesterday. However, as a result of the ruling by the Trial Chamber, it seems that the Defence is now entitled to lead evidence that public buildings including mosques were not targeted. That would, therefore, seem to raise, for the first time, some relevance in relation to whether indeed mosques and other public buildings were targeted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But may I ask you, you're specifically asking for the library. It's not my recollection that the library was as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The basis upon which the Defence submitted to you yesterday that the nontargeting of mosques was relevant was that the nontargeting of such buildings was inconsistent with the existence of a campaign against civilians in Sarajevo. That would seem to, given the ruling, that would seem to open the door as to whether public buildings indeed were targeted, not only under the command period of the accused, but also the period preceding his command. There is a second basis of relevance within that ruling. I anticipate the evidence will be that the great majority of public buildings which had symbolic significance, and I say that mindful of the words of the Defence submission yesterday, were already destroyed by the time that General Galic took over his command. And an evidence of that in light of the ruling yesterday would now seem to be appropriate. In other words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having heard the parties, the objection is denied. So, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you remember the library, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the library. I used to study there while I was at university.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The library was not only shelled but destroyed in 1992, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what was shown on television. I never went there to that location, I mean during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you doubt it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't doubt the fact. Everyone was talking about it. You are talking about it. But I do doubt everything that was shown on that TV, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, the library was not very far from where you lived, was it, no more than say 6 or 7 kilometres at the most?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Less than that, but that was part of the old town into which, after the conflict breakout, it wasn't recommended to go, at least not for the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, I suggest to you that few events in Sarajevo in 1992 were more widely known than the destruction of the library of Sarajevo. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was known. People talked about it. I sometimes doubted. I didn't doubt that it was destroyed, but I didn't go to that area, to that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The library was an important symbol for the people of Sarajevo, wasn't it? It was a source of pride.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I ask the witness be shown a booklet which is opened at a particular page to place on the ELMO. It consists of six colour photographs. I have black and white copies for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Is there a number for that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. The copies which will be the actual exhibit is P3750. To assist the witness and the Trial Chamber, the copy to be shown to the witness is in colour but not to be tendered. In due course, I will provide colour copies to replace the black and white exhibit. In order to assist the Trial Chamber, the page at which the booklet is opened is the second of the three black and white pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, in these photographs, more particularly, in the centre photograph, do we see the library as it was positioned on the banks of Miljacka River?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Following its destruction, were there concerts held in the blackened ruins of the library at various times during the war? In particular, in the chamber that one sees to the centre of the page slightly to the left.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. During the war, I only went once to a concert in a theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You never heard that there was a concert in the library during the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to object. In relation to the relevance, I don't see the connection between these concerts and what the Prosecution is trying to prove.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please respond, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, it makes emphatically the point that the building was important for the -- its symbolic significance to the people of Sarajevo, and even after its destruction, it maintained that significance. And therefore, it is responsive to the Defence contention that buildings one might expect to be targeted as part of a campaign against civilians, in fact, had been targeted. And either destroyed before General Galic commenced his command or were seriously damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Having said that, Mr. President, I'm happy in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. interests of saving time to withdraw the last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if you are happy to do so, please to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The witness has already said he wasn't aware. Perhaps the Court usher could now turn to the second yellow-marked page further on in the booklet and hold it up so I can briefly check that it's the appropriate one. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the building which appears in the photographs before you to be the remains of the post office of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That was shelled in 1992, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when the telephone lines were broken in one part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That was a very important landmark of Sarajevo, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps the Court usher could now turn to the last yellow sticker which is earlier in the booklet. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, I suggest to you that the photographs on the screen at the moment are the remains of a mosque at Kobilja Glava, which was shelled in September of 1992. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know about this. I don't know this building. I never went to Kobilja Glava, and I have no reason not to believe this if you say this is it. But I did not have the opportunity to see this. And I don't know the building so that I could comment on it as I commented on the post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Then might that be returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, moving to another topic, you told us that before you finally decided to leave Sarajevo in July of 1994, you had already left several times during the conflict and after the point that it was difficult to leave. You said that the first time was in April 1993, and you obtained the necessary permissions from the authorities. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When were the other three times, if you could just give us the dates at this stage? I think you said altogether there were four times that you left before you finally left.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until July of the same year, that is, from April to July 1993, and then after that, I was no longer allowed to leave the city which made it difficult for me to carry out the function that I was supposed to do and to carry out the tasks that I was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do I understand you to be telling us that in fact you only left once during the armed conflict before you finally left in July of 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I left four times. I went -- I got out four times, apart from the final departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Do you mean that those four occasions were all between April and July of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. You told us yesterday that on that first occasion, you went to Ilidza and you stayed out of the city for only one hour. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You said that whilst you were out, you learned for the first time that Mojmilo was under the control of the presidency army. Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't be able to say specifically who told me. But just like I knew that the town hall had been set alight, I found out from people talking that Mojmilo was under the control of the presidency forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were you given permission to leave the city for only one hour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a convoy of lorries that was leaving. They were supposed to bring from Kiseljak certain goods. This was the first operation of the newly founded or the renewed Benefactor association, and together with the general secretary of the society, we saw these lorries off so that -- to see them go through the Muslim checkpoint and the Serb checkpoint. And then we returned back into the city, naturally with all the papers, all the documents, that were supposed to be gathered both from the Muslim and from the Serb sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: My question was, were you given permission to leave the city for only one hour? Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no time limit, but it was issued for a particular day. That is, we had to return the same day because the checkpoints had to be notified of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. You told us also --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Mr. President, I think it might be appropriate to move into closed session for the next part of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Private session would do, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I made the same mistake several times. So we now turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yesterday, you told us that humanitarian aid was distributed from a Scouts' centre. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You told us that you personally received humanitarian aid from that centre. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these were personal parcels.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might the witness be shown the map, although I think it's a closed confidential exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it would not be put on the ELMO, I think we could use it. But if you need it to be put on the ELMO, then we should turn into...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, might that be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: While that's being done, sir, you told us there was an incident when you were receiving humanitarian aid in the Scouts' centre when two shells landed on a roof. Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Which humanitarian aid organisation distributed aid at that centre on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Humanitarian aid was expected to arrive of the Serbian charitable society.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was it a aid distribution centre for people who were not of Serbian background as well? That is, Bosnian Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just those of mixed marriages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sorry, are you saying that the only people who attended that centre were people from mixed marriages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Serbs and some from mixed marriages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. And on other occasions, was it a distribution point for aid for Sarajevans generally regardless of their background or their ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just for those who were members of that charitable society.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please mark on the map the place of that Scouts' centre?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marking can only be done, Mr. Ierace, on the ELMO so that we can follow what marking is made. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I had in mind, Mr. President, that if he marked the position with a distinctive letter, we could then place that relevant part on the ELMO without showing the other positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps we will turn into closed session just for one second and have the marking done in closed session. That will prevent us from any mistakes to happen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Closed or private?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think it should be closed because the ELMO will be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, sir, in relation to this incident where two shells landed on the Scouts' centre, you told us yesterday that you later found out that the Scouts' Centre was a military post for a Croatian military outfit. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew before that this was a military facility because I had come -- I had been there before.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The only information -- I'll withdraw that. You told us yesterday that a Croatian soldier there made a comment to the effect "do you know Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. whether they were firing at us or at you?" And you said: "At the time I understood that sarcasm as comment on the fact that there were fierce conflicts between the Muslims and the Croats." Do you remember giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I had said it slightly differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I've just read to you the English translation of your evidence. You, in fact, don't know which forces were responsible for shelling that humanitarian aid distribution, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You also said yesterday that you saw some people wounded from a shelling incident in Vasa Miskin Street. When was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 27th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you actually witness the shelling, or did you arrive at the scene shortly after it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, again, the Defence is objecting here for chronological reasons. I thought that the policy was that at least as far as the shellings were concerned, or the firing, is that we would only focus on the period which is covered by the indictment. In asking questions regarding the period which precedes this period four or five months did not seem acceptable to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I have two bases for asking the question. The first is that much of the evidence which was drawn from this witness yesterday in examination-in-chief in fact focussed on the pre-indictment period. Beyond that, a considerable body of evidence was not distinguished by the Defence as to whether it related to pre-indictment events or during the indictment. To give you one simple example, the witness was asked to indicate positions of certain military units near where he lived, and the question which elicited that information was in relation to the pre-indictment period. Mr. President, the second basis is that the Prosecution case is that the accused assumed responsibility for a pre-existing campaign of shelling and sniping of civilians. So quite separate from the fact that the Defence has thought it proper to elicit such evidence, it's relevant anyway from the indictment itself and from the pretrial brief more particularly of the Prosecution. Perhaps another example is the evidence we've heard as to sniping from the vicinity of the state hospital which clearly is pre-indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may have your leave, I would like us to be very accurate because I believe if we read the transcript carefully we again have one of the counts of the indictment because we are told that the accused would have been responsible as such, that he would have been responsible for a pre-existing campaign of shelling and of sniping. Now, I do not believe that so far the Prosecution had formulated in such a way. And now, what they are trying to prove, responsibility under this form, formulating such a way seems very dangerous to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace told us, at least it's how I understood it, that the accused assumed -- let me just try to find this word. I know that it was the word "assumed." "Assumed responsibility for a pre-existing campaign." I understood that as a campaign did exist, and it was continued, at least that's the words of the Prosecution. I did not understand this to be any extension of the charges against General Galic. I just conferred with my colleague, and both parties have asked questions repeatedly on the pre-indictment period, and both parties have explained that it's of importance to understand the conflict. The Chamber has accepted this several times. It also will accept it now, also under the circumstances just described by the Prosecution. At the same time, the Chamber urges both parties to limit itself in going into too much detail in this period. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, did you arrive after the actual shelling, or did you witness the actual shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately after the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please tell us what you saw.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A horrific picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. I take it there were a number of -- were there a number of bodies on the street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I don't have to, I would ask you, considering my state of mind, going back to that particular incident upsets me a great deal. As far as I understand, Mr. President said here that I am a patient, after all. And really, if there are things that I don't have to say, then I wouldn't go into describing this event because I have a visual memory and it is very upsetting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Approximately how many dead and wounded did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be very hard for me to tell you a figure. I saw mutilated bodies, just at a glance, and it was enough for me not to look any more. It happened right next to the building. If this is closed session, then I may say this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not closed session. But if you think you would tell us something that should be told in closed session, then we first will turn into private session at least so that your words are not available to the outside world.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps before we do that, I could assist perhaps by directing the witness more to the relevant issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There might be another question, so let's first listen to the next question, and then you indicate whether you still would prefer to go into private session or not. If so, please tell me. If not, just answer the question. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you where it happened. I'm asking you for some indication as to the number of casualties; in other words, the approximate number of dead and wounded that you saw. If I could help you, was it more or less than ten, whatever the number was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read in the papers officially the number published was that there were more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. How many did you read in the paper?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did I understand your answer well that you said that the newspapers reported a number higher than ten? Because that's what you were asked, whatever the number might have been. Then may I ask you, was that in conformity with your own observations of what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not in a position to count. I saw a scene, and I find it very difficult to look at blood anyway, not even an injection. I find it hard. So immediately after that horrific event, I entered a building which was nearby, so I didn't see, I could not have seen the number of people who died. In any case, at that time, the area was cordoned off so you were not able to come close to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did it appear to you that the victims were civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And there was talk about -- that these were civilians who had been in a queue waiting for bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did it appear to you, from what you could see, that they had been deliberately targeted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to claim either way yes or no. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was it consistent with your observations that they were civilians who had been in a queue at the time that they were shelled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some who were there, they told me that it was a queue for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You, at that time, were a civilian. These people were civilians. You were told they had been queueing for bread. What thoughts did you have for your personal safety in those circumstances as you saw that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fear is an integral part of man's life, of one's way of life and thought. And there is nobody who is free from fear under wartime conditions. So in our case, everybody, and me, of course, included, experienced fear, different kinds of fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You've told us that it appeared to you the victims were civilians as opposed to combatants. You have made abundantly clear to us that today, ten years later, you were traumatized --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure that this testimony, that the witness has said civilian as opposed to a combatant. That is, we all know in the beginning of the war especially, there were -- that a majority of civilians were combatants, so when we talk about these terms, combatant, I mean, the witness did not use this term, and I'm afraid that it causes a confusion; hence the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It seems that Mr. Ierace added something when he told the witness that the victims had a civilian appearance, and it also seems that Mr. Piletta-Zanin seems to forget that the question was about the appearance, and not about persons that would have both qualities but showed only one at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm happy to withdraw the question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please, then, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Mr. President, I just want to clarify as to whether it's private session or open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we have not moved into private session because the witness asked for it and then you did put an additional question to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you told us that there were occasions when civilians were stopped on the streets of Sarajevo and their identification was checked by officials. Did that ever happen to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did, a number of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. And were you ever, your identity, your identification papers having been checked, taken to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't taken to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You've told us --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this stage I think we need to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Being in open session, I'll repeat my question to you whether there's any need to re-examine the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And to the Witness, good afternoon once again. I'd like first to make something quite clear. In the first place with regard to the library building that was mentioned earlier, this library, is it far from the central post office building? As far as I know, the building that you saw some time ago, and do you know how far the two buildings are from each other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a kilometre and something perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Right. Can you tell us which are official buildings behind the library, if there were any, that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'd like to go to the post office. You told us that after that shelling, the telephone lines were cut off. So my question is as follows: To your knowledge, which is the neighbourhood or neighbourhoods which were affected by that particular shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, it was the post office building. It was next to the Miljacka, from the building. And if it was shelled as people said in Sarajevo, that it had been shelled, then it could have been targeted directly from what I know. But I do not know which area might have been affected by that shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, we are now in the early conflict days. Do you know which means of communication did the groups of combatants in Sarajevo use?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. That does not arise out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I respond, because in the witness's answer to the question concerning the shelling of the post office building, this witness said that immediately after that, telephone communication stopped. So the witness says that in times of peace are civilian, but in times are military --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. He also said exactly the same thing when he was examined in chief, so the Defence was aware of that at that stage as well. And if needs be, I can find the reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not have the -- that specific part in my mind. But let me just see whether it's of any use what we are doing. Do you have any knowledge of the communication between the combatants, different groups of combatants? Do you have any knowledge on how they communicated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I know what I saw in front of the building that I lived in. As a rule, they had Motorolas with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But do you know anything about the functioning of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the witness now testified that he knows that Motorolas were used, and he also answered that he has no specific knowledge on the functioning of the communications. If there's any specific other question you'd like to ask, then one or two specifically on the subject and directly related to what happened to the post office. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So the post office and the telephones. Do we agree on that, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, the issue was about the post office, and of course telephones. But then of course we're not talking about Motorolas. We are then talking about fixed telephone lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can give you that page reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you could give it to me, then I --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It's page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What day? Was it yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yesterday, page 13.311 at line 2. "Q. Could you tell us, when we spoke about the facilities, could you tell us whether during the war telephones operated in Sarajevo during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the part of Sarajevo where I lived for a while, there was no -- there were no telephones that were operating because the central post office was destroyed. So it was clearly raised and dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall move to another subject, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to go now to the mortar, the mobile mortar that you saw with your own eyes. Will you tell us in what state -- what state of mind was your wife when she came to tell you about it and to invite you to look at that mortar? Will you describe to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: His evidence is not that that his wife came to tell him about it, rather that she called out from where she was, as I understood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we first clarify this. The testimony is not such that the one would exclude the other. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, how did this episode unfold? You told us, at least that is how I understood it, that your wife told you that a mortar was firing from a truck. Now, how did you receive this information? Could you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a very hard time, and there were very -- and there were much more important things for me to pay attention to details. But in Sarajevo, there were this general belief that one should disappear from the area where television cameras turned up because something was about to happen there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Excuse me, sorry. But what we want to know is how did you learn about this, to earn the time? Did your wife call out to you? Did she come to you or what? Just this short phase, how did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: She came to fetch me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Mr. President, that is what I believe I understood from the language, and we frequently have these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When your wife, therefore, came to look for you, Witness, what kind of state was she in? Could you describe it to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object. I draw your attention to the testimony from yesterday, page 13.276, at line 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "It was late afternoon, and..." I'm just missing. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is examination-in-chief. And these questions do not arise out of cross-examination. The witness gave that explanation then as to what happened on this point. So my fundamental objection is that the fact that an issue is dealt with in cross-examination doesn't mean that the party calling the witness can revisit that issue in a general sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree. But the first question was just to clarify an issue before we would have a next question because there might have been some confusion about. And therefore, this first question is in order to clarify the issue. And let me just read what is on the line you just quoted. It reads: "It was late afternoon, and they called out to me to come and see how mortar was firing shots." That's what the testimony was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And in my view, but I could misunderstand, and perhaps should confer with my colleague first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both Judges, not being native English speakers, understand this line such that that they called out to me to come and see does not exclude that those who called out were visible for the person that was called out. So it does not exclude in the view of the Judges that this person -- well, let's say it not necessarily means that this calling out was done from such a distance that the witness could not have seen the persons calling out. And I think the next question, and that was what it was all about, is the state of mind of his wife. And that, I would say, responds to an issue that was very specifically dealt with in cross-examination; that was the -- so the Chamber would allow such questions, but to a limited extent. We are here confronted with a situation where an issue had been dealt with with some superficiality and then was dealt with in great depth in cross-examination. That would allow for some additional questions for the Defence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. But if this will put the Prosecution's mind at ease, we shall be quite happy if you ask those questions concerning the state of mind of the witness's wife. If not, then the Defence will ask those questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber allows you to put some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, will you tell us, at the time when you learned that fact from the mouth of your wife, in what state was she in? What state of mind was she in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think she looked normal and slightly frightened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I move on, but in relation to these same things, another fact which emerged during your cross-examination, and that is the existence of alarms. You spoke to us about alarms. I shall move to a different channel. You spoke to us about alarms, whether the alarms, whether the sirens, whether they were used regularly. And if yes, in relation to what? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were alarm -- the car alarms which when shooting or detonations exploded on some cars, then they would switch on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, are you telling us about mobile alarms? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I think there is some confusion. Were you talking about theft alarms as you usually find them on private cars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But these alarms, what were they meant for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To protect against car theft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did I understand you well that because of perhaps the air pressure or of a mortar being fired, at least an explosion close by, that cars would shake a little bit and then the alarms would get off?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I'm moving to another line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You spoke to us about your friend who was a doctor. Don't mention his name. Who was wounded by, as he told you, by a neighbour. Now, the question is as follows: Did he tell you the ethnic background of that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. neighbour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one could guess it, but he didn't give a name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. If this is something that one can guess, what were you supposed to be able to guess in your understanding of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object. That question has no proper basis, Mr. President. Witness has indicated that he wasn't told. And from that point on, it becomes entirely speculative. For a start, there has been no suggestion of motive for the shooting. It would be extraordinary to conclude from the bare fact that a person was shot by a neighbour that one could deduce what the ethnic background of a neighbour was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the objection is sustained. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you told us several times about how difficult for you it was to find streets because their names have changed. Was it done systematically or are you talking about two or three exceptions, for instance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost all. There are no streets with names of Serbs, named after Serbs. And before the war, there were quite a number of them in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness has repeatedly expressed his difficulty in finding streets because of the change of names. And it's not something that we heard for the first time in cross-examination. So there would have been ample opportunity to ask this in chief. Please proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you spoke to us of what happened in May 1992, and you told us that you only had a glimpse, a fleeting look at the scene, and it nevertheless brought back to mind very painful pictures, images. But did you perhaps watch television or journalists who were present at that moment who were near the scene of that incident or at the scene of the incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could see it later on on the screens, and that was in the wake of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And according to what you could see on your screens immediately after the scene, was it what you had seen, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any reason whatsoever to think that you may know who the authors of this attack could be?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: "Do you have reason whatsoever" does not -- invites a range of speculation. Secondly, the question goes to responsibility. I don't recall that cross-examination ventured into the area of knowledge of responsibility, or indeed responsibility. Therefore, the question does not arise from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm going to respond in the following manner: Formally, no, but practically, yes because the reason why Mr. Ierace was authorised to continue his line of questioning, consistently saying that there was a shelling campaign that preceded that a posteriori will imply the responsibility --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I withdraw that objection, Mr. President, and would seek leave to ask further questions in cross-examination. And if you find against me on the first basis of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The subject is not forbidden ground, but would you please ask clear questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think your first question was whether he has any knowledge. That would allow him to tell this Chamber who was -- who had been firing the projectile that caused the events he observed. I think that's the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this was a shell, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But who could have caused the attack?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, not who could have caused. Everyone in the world could have done that. Do you have any knowledge, Mr. DP1, who fired --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just from what I read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not from your own knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, just from what I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please move to your next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I just have to confer for one minute. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Mr. Ierace, are you intending to ask leave to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No. At some stage before the witness is dismissed, there is something which I wish to raise in closed session, perhaps in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of the witness. Then I'd like to ask, there's one issue still to be raised before you will be excused, Mr. DP1. So I would like you to leave this courtroom for a while so that the parties can tell the Chamber what they want to tell the Chamber, and then you would return and that would then finally conclude your examination, perhaps. Madam usher, would you please escort the witness out of the courtroom. Would private session do, Mr. Ierace? Then we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP1, this concludes your evidence in this Court. May I first tell you that it would improper to discuss with any of the persons you mentioned, whether you know them well, whether they are good friends, whether they are not good friends, to discuss with any of these persons your testimony in this Court. So the Court orders you to refrain from doing that. And then my last words will be that we are quite aware that it's a long trip to come from your country, come to the Hague. You've testified for three consecutive days. You've answered the questions of the parties. We will now see whether there were any additional questions to be put to you by the Court because that's what I had forgotten. But it's always better to find out even in a late stage. So there might be some additional questions from the Judges now. And once you've answered them, I'm going to thank you for giving answers to all these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] If you would, Witness, just a couple of points that I would like to have clarified for my own information. I believe that you said in your testimony that you were leaving -- you left the house more or less every day, and you said that you had arranged a convoy, that you had been involved in organising the second convoy that left the city. Now, my question is the following: The petrol, how did you find it? At the time, did you have a vehicle, or -- yes, could you please answer about petrol.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have a vehicle. And at that time, apart from people with privileges, nobody was driving a car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private persons, you mean military persons, civilians, high officials? What do you mean by "private persons"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, just the people you've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You said that there were some -- there were soldiers in uniform. You mentioned the categories of soldiers. And if I understood you correctly, there were at least one unit under the command of Juka Prazina, which was -- they were dressed in black. And you also mentioned some other units that were in camouflage uniforms, and some other who had or wore Green Berets, if I'm not mistaken. Now, were all soldiers in uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I was able to see, and those who entered the buildings that they were quartered in, a large number of troops gathered in a very popular cafe in Sarajevo which was practically open throughout the war. And they went there for -- in their spare time, and they were dressed accordingly. And that's when I saw these different uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see. And you also said in relation to the barricades that there were civilians who were holding these barricades, these civilians. Now, how did you conclude that these were civilians? How did you assess that? Was it according to what they were wearing? Were they not bearing arms? Were they not carrying arms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to start with, and throughout the month of May, there were many checkpoints in all the areas in the city. At that time, I only had one route. It was just over a kilometre to my work. And at first, there were two, then four, and then later on just one checkpoint. When people who, as I understood, who wore civilian clothes, they would do checks, and they were always accompanied by a person who was armed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean policemen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, another topic, please. You said in answer to a question that you were asked, you said in relation to the destruction, you said that before July, before you definitely left Sarajevo, you used the term, and I will use the term in English which was used, that there was "much destruction." Now, could you please, if you remember, do you make a distinction between destruction that occurred in the city in the months of May, June, July 1992 and after this period, following this period? When you say that there was "much destruction" are you talking about systematic destruction, which went on throughout the "conflict," or are you making a distinction between that period and another period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do make a distinction. What I said was that there wasn't much destruction in the part of town where I lived in relation to what I saw when I went to Ilidza for the first time. However, I also said where there were front lines, everything was scorched. And the real destruction I only saw when I went to the airport and I went out to the airport on several occasions for talks. And on that part of the front line, there was much destruction, extreme destruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my question was whether do you have an idea about distinguishing between one period and another? You said -- when you say there was much destruction, are you saying that this was throughout the period? Was it from May until July 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, and the way I felt it, the fiercest period, the fiercest period of conflict, May, June, July, August, and even September of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise. Just a very brief question. In relation to your friend who was wounded by a bullet and that you went to visit in the hospital, I understand that he didn't tell you the name of his neighbour. But did he tell you if this person was a soldier, a military person, or a civilian, or somebody that he had some dispute with? Did he touch upon the subject at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will allow me, I would like to just elaborate a little and answer you with precision. But if you don't want me to elaborate, I can tell you that he didn't tell me neither. He simply told me that he had been hit. He had been shot at by his neighbour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you as well. You told us about trenches you had observed. I remember that you said ones in the Stup area and ones on Trebevic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were these the only times you personally saw the trenches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us with more precision at what distance approximately you observed them? As I understood, you were in a car at both occasions. Was it just next to the road or was it at a distance, or could you inform us about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering that both times, the vehicle was shot at, that is, the lorry that I was in was fired at, instinctively, I turned away because the door was shot at off the vehicle that I was in. And then with amazement, I realised that the demarcation line between the warring parties -- well, I couldn't tell you exactly, completely accurately, within a metre. But it wasn't even 50 or 70 metres away because the lorry was high and I was able to see the line that -- how shall I put it, camouflaged partly also because of the rain, it was possible to see the soil, the ground. And I saw that as I was returning from Belgrade because on one occasion, during the war, I had gone to Belgrade. And the second time at the Stupska Petlja, I also had occasion to see something because I had a very odd meeting with a BH Army soldier, an out-of-the-ordinary meeting. I had the opportunity to see within a few metres a shelter, or rather the place that this soldier was in because he showed it to me. Saying that myself and all of the others on the other side of the road should be eliminated because he was constantly being shelled in this location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
