utterances.text: So the second time you got off the car, and that's when you saw the trenches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You described military people in the trenches. You talked about camouflage uniforms when you were referring to Trebevic. You were referring to a soldier when you were talking about Stupska Petlja, I think. I hope I pronounce it well. Did you see any civilians at these times, in the trenches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You also testified that civilians were rounded up and that even one friend of you had to dig trenches for nine months at Trebevic. Did you observe this personally, or is it what he told you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a colleague of mine from when we were students. We used to share a room. He was a cello player, and I saw his hands that was just an old oak tree. That's what his hands looked like. I asked him: "What happened to you?" And he told me on a daily basis for nine months he had been going to dig the trenches. I have already given you the name. I wouldn't like to repeat it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We don't have to repeat it. So do I understand you well that if you are talking about civilians that had to dig trenches, that what you told us is what you were told that had happened since you described two occasions where you personally saw trenches without any civilians and even kept by military people at that moment, but many other occasions you told us about, that is, what you heard, what other people told you about civilians digging trenches? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. With the observation that I know specific people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course. It's not just general stories but what specific people told you. Thank you very much for your answers. I see that -- I wanted to start a thank you but it's not easy because it seems that both parties have additional questions. But I think it would be first for Mr. Piletta-Zanin. But, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, as you know, it should be directly following from the subject covered by the questions of the Judges. So if you first put your question to the witness, and then...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. My question is in relation to a question that you asked about the trenches that were observed by the witness and the possible presence of the civilians in the trenches. Do you allow me to ask this question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, there was nothing new in this question that was not covered by the -- the reason I asked this question was the witness testified about civilians digging trenches. And at the same time, he testified on what he personally saw or not. I just verified whether the information he gave was correct or not. So -- but let me first confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You know this is a very liberal Chamber now and then. If you would put that question, then we'll consider whether the witness should answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much indeed. The question would be the following.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the trenches that you were able to observe on two occasions, were they already finished, or were they in the process of being dug?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, they were not in the process of being dug. They were part of the front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Mr. President. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, is there any additional question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You said in response to the question from Judge Orie that on one of the occasions that you observed the trenches, you were returning from Belgrade. At that time that you made the observation of the trenches, were you on the Bosnian Serb army side of the trenches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The front line, the way I saw it, where I saw the soldiers was actually the road, part of the road, which led -- which went or ran along Trebevic and alongside was the front line of the BH Army. So I was returning on my way back. I was sitting on the right-hand side because the driver was on the left-hand side. Then I sat. That's how I saw the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Quite simply, I'm asking you were you on the Bosnian Serb army side of the trenches? In other words, of the confrontation line, when you saw the trenches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The road, yes, the road went on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. In relation to the second time you saw the trenches, were you on the Bosnian Serb side or on the side of the presidency forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on the side of the Army of the BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you. Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. DP1, it is always difficult for this Chamber to finally conclude the examination. You have been here for so long. You have come from so far. I'd like to thank you for coming to The Hague. You've answered all the questions, not only of the parties but also of the Judges. And it's important for us to hear the testimony of those who have been present during the relevant times and the relevant places. And I would like to thank you for that. Thank you for coming. Madam usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll just take one minute to indicate to the parties what the Chamber intends to do after the break. I'll first go through a few outstanding issues, but very briefly, I'm not in a position to say to the parties that they should answer yes or no. But if it would come as close to that, it would be much appreciated. Then before we start the examination of the next witness, first, a decision has to be taken in respect of this witness. And therefore, we will for some time be in closed session, and I'll explain exactly what we'll do, closed session then. But we'll follow to some extent a suggestion made yesterday. The final thing I'd like now to do is deal with the exhibits of Witness DP1 and then have a break until 10 minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1700, under seal, pseudonym sheet. Exhibit D1755 under seal, map marked by witness. Exhibit P3750, photos of various buildings in Sarajevo, black and white.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did I understand that you wanted to tender the original coloured ones? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That's an original exhibit, Mr. President. At this stage, the black and white, and when we receive a colour copy, I'll change them over. I'll seek to change them over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So at this very moment, it's black and white, and then it will be colour. And then we will adjourn until 10 minutes past 6.00. I apologise for the interpreters that we went on a bit longer; on the other hand, the next term will be shorter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not because I have difficulties in refinding my rhythm, but because we needed 20 minutes to consider whether the exhibits were admitted into evidence. They are admitted since there were no objections. Before we continue with the examination of the next witness, I would like to go through a list of issues very quickly, just in order to make sure that there are no major outstanding difficulties. We discussed at an earlier stage the 130 entries on the exhibit list that were not at that time yet disclosed. Has this matter been solved, or has it not?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the documents that were not on the exhibit lists were put on the additional list of the 8th of October, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would have been my second question. But my first question was whether the entries on the exhibit list that were not yet disclosed, and there was some confusion about whether or not they were disclosed or not, whether there have been any additional copies made. I think that's on the 130 pages where I indicated I would copy them myself if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have done all that. I mean, my learned friend is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We are still in the process of checking those documents, Mr. President. There were some more documents provided by the Defense, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I had 130 written down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There were two lists, the 130, and then there were an additional 85 documents provided which didn't seem to be on the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the second issue just raised. And although I have not seen it yet, but I was informed that an additional list has been filed so that documents disclosed did not appear yet on the list do appear now on the list, at least there's an additional list on which they might appear. And I take it that you continue checking --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. We have no complaint at this stage, Mr. President, on either of those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what the Chamber likes to hear. Then we had problem about four books, five books, six books. Has that problem been solved?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It transpired, I think, that there were five not six, and again we have received some further information from the Defence, and we have no complaint at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No complaints. Okay, that's fine. Then there was a problem in reaching, or at least finding the addresses of some witnesses, some suggestions were made by the Prosecution how to find these addresses. These were, I would say, international witnesses. Has this -- has any progress been made in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The Defence sent us a letter listing I think it was about six people, most of whom are military. We haven't yet responded to that letter other than the suggestion made in open court that they approach the militaries. I will respond to that letter and update that with specific information if we have it. And I'll do that this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Then there was an issue of the authenticity of documents on the Defence lists, the authenticity problem was that the Prosecution sought ways to be informed about the sources of these documents, and they were not fully satisfied with Banja Luka as a possible source because according to the information the Prosecution got, the documents were deposited at Banja Luka coming from the Defence, so therefore there was a request to contact the investigators of the Defence. Has any progress been made in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. It was discussed at a meeting with the Defence last Friday and also this week, and there hasn't been any progress made on that. We have made clear to the Defence what we require, the details of where each document was obtained, sufficient detail, to enable the Prosecution to go to those places and make its own inquiries so it can satisfy itself that the documents indeed are authentic. We had proposed the idea of the investigators meeting. We're told that the Defence investigator will next be in The Hague on the 17th of October. I am not confident that that meeting will achieve the purpose. It seems to me that the appropriate way, if the Defence wishes to take all reasonable steps to secure our agreement as to the authenticity, the appropriate method is for the Defence tell us in writing where each exhibit was obtained from in that sufficient detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pilipovic, I saw you nodding no, that's just for the transcript. But could you please respond.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we discussed this problem at the two meetings that we had, and in principle, I believe we agreed that investigators should meet. Now that the request of the Defence should inform the -- our learned friends in writing where the documents have come from, I think I have repeated several times that it was [indiscernible] Nevesinje, Trebinje, but had my learned friends asked me in time, they said they needed it in writing, then we would have done that. But we have agreed in principle that investigators should meet, if my memory serves me well. And we also met on Monday and last week, and that was our understanding. But if you want the Defence to submit in writing, that presents no problem. But my learned friends did not put such a request to us in advance. The request was that the investigators meet and we agreed that it would happen, and I already said that I believe the investigator of the Defence will be coming to The Hague on the 17th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There still seems to be some confusion or disagreement on how to solve it. As I indicated last week, if the parties do not solve it, there will be a meeting. That means that that meeting will take place tomorrow at 12.00, unless the parties have informed me by 11.00 that the problem has been solved. I see that both parties seem to have come close to each other, and there might be some misunderstanding, if there's no misunderstanding but just disagreement, it's useful that the meeting takes place. If there's no disagreement, you've got two hours tomorrow morning to find out that there's no disagreement, and you can spare yourself the time to meet with me, or with the senior legal officer. Next issue is whether any progress has been made in compromising on stipulated facts. Perhaps I'll now ask first to Mr. Piletta-Zanin or Ms. Pilipovic to deal with that, and then ask for Mr. Ierace to respond. Any progress made?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, the first question about tomorrow's meeting at noon, could the Prosecution please provide the interpretation services because last time it didn't go well. So as for the second thing, we suggested --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just, it's a meeting on the request of the Chamber. So the Chamber will decide whether there's a need for translation during this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the presence of at least one counsel who speaks and understands one of the official languages of the Tribunal is specifically in order to make sure that whenever there's any need for an untranslated communication, that it will be possible without losing any rights for the Defence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We have not made now any progress regarding the stipulated facts. We only talked about a procedure which would mean that the Prosecution tells us what they think. That would not have to be in dispute from their point of view, and then we would answer, yes, we accept this, we cannot accept that, and so on and so forth. And it seems that the methodology does not seem to be agreeable to the Prosecution, so at the moment, we are -- it seems that we are at an impasse.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would be grateful for the assistance of the Trial Chamber on that issue as well. Prior to the commencement of the trial, the Prosecution's -- well, I personally spent in excess of 20 hours with the Defence putting forward facts for their consideration. That exercise did not end well. I have said to the Defence that now that the Prosecution has presented its case, perhaps they can indicate to us which parts of the case they agree with. And the response has been, well, no, even though we've presented our case, it's for us to guess what is agreed and for us to put to them what should be agreed. I don't think there's any prospect of the parties advancing the agreed facts beyond what was filed in November. But perhaps with the assistance of the Trial Chamber, we could accelerate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's meet tomorrow morning at 9.00 and discuss this issue, either with the senior legal officer or myself. Tomorrow morning, 9.00, we see whether any progress can be made between the parties. The Chamber will inform you about the place where we'll meet. It might be in my chambers. Then another issue, a very technical one, is that the Defence has asked for videolink, although it was categorised as a protective measure, I think videolink is not a protective measure. So we can deal with it in open session. In the submission made on the 20th of September, it was indicated that the videolink would be needed between the 25th of October and the 6th of November. In the request for protective measures, we find that the videolink would be needed between the 28th of October, which is three days later, up until the 1st of November. And -- and that's what causes the problems, be at two different places, one in Belgrade and one in Sarajevo. For technical reasons it might not be possible to have a videolink on two different locations -- so it's not possible to have videolinks in two places in such a short period of time, so the Defence is invited to reschedule, especially the videolink witnesses and to keep in close contact with the registry. Just inform you, the transfer of the videolink from Belgrade to Sarajevo would need at least two days. So the schedule has to be adapted in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before we leave that topic, the Prosecution has not yet formally responded to that, but I can say this: That the Prosecution was required to obtain medical certificates and the like in order to substantiate its request for videolink. The basis for the Defence request in every case, I think, is health problems. We have not seen any medical reports. It might expedite matters if you thought it appropriate at this stage that medical reports be obtained. I note that two of the witnesses are in wheelchairs. One of the Prosecution witnesses was in a wheelchair and gave live evidence. But again, it may be that the Prosecution won't take a hard approach on that, but we simply need proper substantiating material. And I appreciate we're in open session, but being a little circumspect, having regard to some of the names, I think it would be entirely appropriate to have that medical evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This was not a decision on the request of videolink. I hope that that's clear. But I just pointed at some technical problems if the Chamber would allow for the -- for a videolink. We are still considering the reasons. And of course, we'll give a decision in due course. But just to inform the Defence that the Chamber remembers that once when videolink was asked for some person that had underwent surgery, the Chamber wants to have further information as to the kind of surgery and the time of recovery needed to be moving around again. So that, of course, that's also the reason why it takes a bit more time that the Chamber tries to compare carefully what we asked from the Prosecution in order to ask not more but not less from the Defence as well. That's the videolink, especially the technical, on whether the request would be granted. Yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I understand that the videolink will depend on the Chamber's decision. What I wish to say, however, is the Defence would like to have all the videolink witnesses in Sarajevo. And I think that should be the 4th and the 5th of November. That was Monday and Tuesday. And if need be, we shall provide the medical recommendation. Our learned friends have not told us that they require that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In general, you could expect that the Chamber would choose, unless there are differences, the same attitude to the Defence as we did to the Prosecution. And of course, if the Prosecution provided some information, there was no need to ask for it. So perhaps you could orient yourself also on what information was provided without being asked for it by the Chamber. So you would say you would concentrate anyhow on Sarajevo. That would at least make things less complicated. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. One of the witnesses is an invalid. He's in a wheelchair, and it really would be very difficult for him, and he would also need somebody to -- he would also need a companion, and I think it would be too expensive for him to come to The Hague. The second one has a heart condition, and the third one has high sugar. We thought he would be a live witness here, however because of his health complaints --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you prepare for the proper information, that if the Chamber would ask you to provide it, that it will be there. Let's not discuss now the details because that's not the purpose of this short -- it's not a formal Status Conference but it looks a bit like. I would like to turn into closed session. Private session will do. I am making the same mistakes again and again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. We are in open session now as far as I can see it. Is it something you'd like to raise in open session or?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because what we were thinking is that it would be useful to go the other way around regarding the witnesses because I'm not going to be here on Friday. This is something that we can discuss out of court. And if there is some agreement that we can come to, we will certainly inform your Chamber immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's about the witnesses and protective measures or?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is just to change the order of the two witnesses regarding our preparations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's not entirely clear to me, to be quite honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, just simply, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I haven't got the order in my mind, but I do understand that you want to change the order of appearance of two witnesses. And has the Prosecution been informed about it? They have not been informed about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, that was the point that we were going to look at at a later time. It would be number 3 instead of number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so that's what you suggest. And what you inform the Prosecution about at this very moment. Okay, we'll see whether there comes any response. If there's nothing else, we'll adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00 in this same courtroom, but we might see each other at an earlier time tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: at 7.02 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 10th day of October, 2002, at 2.15 p.m. 22 23 24 25
